To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transition from HCS toward committed progenitors is associated with the downregulation of HSC-specific and developmental genes and the upregulation of lineage-specific and immune-regulatory genes.
the expression of a large number (about 50%) of genes in the hematopoietic hierarchy is regulated during the transition from HCS to downstream progenitor cells.

(1) HSCs and downstream progenitors have different transcriptional programs; (2) HSCs are characterized by a large number of up-regulated genes, whereas downstream progenitors are characterized by a small number of up-regualted genes; and (3) the HSC-associated genes include many developmentally regulated and previously identified self-renewal genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the molecular mechanisms that regulate hematopoietic cell fate decisions, with particular focus on the mechanisms controlling the balance between self-renewal and differentiation of HSCs.

the molecular characterization of the HSC and its transition into lineage-committed progenitors, and with identifying the molecular mechanisms that regulate self-renewal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HSCs are transcriptionally active, and their unique self-renewal properties are associated with the expression of a specific gene profile, distinct from that of downstream progenitors.
HSCs and progenitors have distinct gene expression signatures, and the transition between these two cell types is accompanied by a gradual change in the expression pattern of a number of genes.

HSCs are a distinct population of cells that express a unique set of genes that are associated with self-renewal, and that the transcriptional program of HSCs changes as they transition toward more committed progenitors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the transition from stem cells toward committed progenitors is associated with a progressive loss of stem cell-specific genes and acquisition of lineage-specific genes and that the HSCs express many developmentally regulated transcripts, suggesting that HSCs are in an activated state.
HSCs are characterized by the expression of a large number (about 600) of genes, many of which are not expressed in more committed progenitors.
the transcriptional status of hematopoietic cells is a function of their differentiation status.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HSCs are a unique cell population that has a distinct gene signature and that the transition from HCS to downstream progenitors correlates with a progressive down-regulation of HSC-associated transcripts and up-regulation of lineage-specific transcripts.
